findings.explanation: The new `where_in` Jinja filter (superset/jinja_context.py:404-420) builds a SQL IN-clause by string-concatenating user-controlled values. For non-string values it calls `str(value)` with no quoting or escaping, and for strings it only escapes the single quote character (mark) via `value.replace(mark, mark*2)`. The values come from `filter_values`/`get_filters` (superset/jinja_context.py:201-240), which return raw filter values from the request/form data. The rendered output is returned as raw SQL by `process_template` (superset/jinja_context.py:462-473) and executed. Because the escaping is a hand-written, dialect-agnostic single-quote doubling (not the dialect-aware `String().literal_processor` used elsewhere, e.g. line 194), and non-string values are emitted unquoted, an attacker who controls a filter value can break out of the intended literal and inject arbitrary SQL. The filter is registered on the SandboxedEnvironment used by all template processors (line 456) and is documented for use with `filter_values` (docs/docs/installation/sql-templating.mdx:209,248).

findings.suggested_fix: Do not hand-roll SQL quoting. Build the IN-clause using the database dialect's literal processor (e.g. SQLAlchemy `String().literal_processor(dialect)` / `sqlalchemy.sql.expression.literal`) for each value, or better, avoid embedding values in SQL text entirely by using bound parameters. At minimum, restrict `where_in` to scalar primitives (int/float/bool/str), escape using the target dialect's quoting rules for every value type, and reject/raise on non-scalar or non-serializable values rather than calling `str(value)`.
